clinicalPearls: A myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by autonomous overproduction of red cells, often with raised white cells and platelets
Almost all cases carry a JAK2 mutation (V617F or exon 12)
Symptoms include aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia, headache, plethora and thrombosis
A low serum erythropoietin supports the diagnosis and helps distinguish it from secondary polycythaemia
The dominant risks are arterial and venous thrombosis, with later potential to transform to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia
Management combines venesection to a target haematocrit, aspirin and, in higher-risk patients, cytoreduction
reference.pathophysiology: Polycythaemia vera is a clonal stem cell disorder driven in nearly all cases by activating JAK2 mutations, which render erythroid (and often myeloid and megakaryocytic) progenitors hypersensitive to, or independent of, erythropoietin. The resulting unregulated proliferation expands the red cell mass and frequently the granulocyte and platelet lines. The elevated haematocrit raises blood viscosity and, together with qualitative platelet and endothelial changes, produces the high thrombotic risk, while progressive marrow fibrosis or clonal evolution underlies transformation.
additionalDifferentials: Relative (apparent) polycythaemia from plasma volume contraction
additionalInvestigations: JAK2 V617F and, if negative, exon 12 mutation analysis
redFlags: Arterial or venous thrombosis, including unusual-site thrombosis
Very high haematocrit with hyperviscosity symptoms
Progressive splenomegaly or cytopenias suggesting transformation to myelofibrosis
reference.prognosis: With haematocrit control and thrombosis prevention many patients live for decades, but the disease carries thrombotic risk and a smaller long-term risk of transformation to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia.
pitfalls: Confusing it with secondary or relative polycythaemia
Failing to control the haematocrit to target
Overlooking JAK2-negative cases needing exon 12 testing
Missing transformation signalled by new cytopenias or splenomegaly
management: Venesection to a target haematocrit to reduce blood viscosity and thrombotic risk, the cornerstone of treatment
Low-dose aspirin for all patients without contraindication to lower arterial and venous thrombotic risk
Cytoreductive therapy, with hydroxycarbamide first-line or interferon particularly in younger patients and pregnancy, for high-risk patients
Ruxolitinib, a JAK inhibitor, for hydroxycarbamide-resistant or intolerant disease and troublesome symptoms
Symptom control for aquagenic pruritus and erythromelalgia, with optimisation of cardiovascular risk factors
Monitor full blood count and haematocrit and surveil for progression to myelofibrosis or leukaemic transformation
Refer to haematology for pregnancy, thrombosis or evidence of disease transformation

valueTables.title: Diseases associated with massive splenomegaly
valueTables.footnote: Massive splenomegaly means the spleen extends more than 8 cm below the left costal margin and/or weighs more than 1000 g.

cells.text: Hemoconcentration secondary to dehydration, diuretics, ethanol abuse, androgens or tobacco abuse
Carbon monoxide intoxication; high oxygen-affinity hemoglobin; high altitude; pulmonary disease; right to left cardiac or vascular shunts; sleep apnea syndrome; hepatopulmonary syndrome
Renal artery stenosis; focal sclerosing or membranous glomerulonephritis; postrenal transplantation; renal cysts; Bartter's syndrome
Hypernephroma; hepatoma; cerebellar hemangioblastoma; uterine myoma; adrenal tumors; meningioma; pheochromocytoma
